reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: A rare inherited (autosomal recessive) autonomic disorder in which noradrenaline and adrenaline cannot be synthesised, leaving dopamine as the released catecholamine
Presents with profound orthostatic hypotension from infancy or childhood, often with perinatal complications such as hypotension, hypoglycaemia, and hypothermia
The biochemical hallmark is very low or undetectable plasma noradrenaline and adrenaline with markedly raised plasma dopamine, giving a high dopamine-to-noradrenaline ratio
Ptosis, nasal stuffiness, retrograde ejaculation, and exercise intolerance are characteristic
Sweating is relatively preserved because sudomotor fibres are cholinergic, distinguishing it from some other forms of autonomic failure
Uniquely, it can be treated by replacing the deficient product with the synthetic precursor droxidopa, which is converted directly to noradrenaline and bypasses the missing enzyme
Should be considered in a young patient with severe orthostatic hypotension and a characteristic catecholamine profile
Supportive management follows autonomic-failure principles: volume and salt expansion, compression garments, and physical counter-manoeuvres
reference.pathophysiology: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is the enzyme that converts dopamine to noradrenaline within sympathetic nerve terminals and the adrenal medulla. In dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency, biallelic loss-of-function variants abolish enzyme activity, so noradrenaline and adrenaline cannot be produced and dopamine is released instead from sympathetic nerves. The absence of noradrenergic vasoconstriction causes severe orthostatic hypotension, while excess circulating dopamine may contribute to renal and other effects. Parasympathetic and cholinergic sympathetic (sudomotor) functions, which do not depend on this enzyme, are preserved. Because the defect is a single missing biosynthetic step, supplying a precursor that is decarboxylated directly to noradrenaline can restore noradrenergic signalling.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited catecholamine-biosynthesis or aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase disorders
Menkes disease with copper-dependent enzyme dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Supine and standing plasma catecholamines showing absent noradrenaline and adrenaline with raised dopamine
Calculation of the plasma dopamine-to-noradrenaline ratio
Head-up tilt-table testing to quantify the orthostatic hypotension
Genetic testing of the DBH gene
Assessment of sudomotor (sweating) function to demonstrate its relative preservation
redFlags: Neonatal or infantile hypotension, hypoglycaemia, and collapse
Severe exercise intolerance limiting daily function
reference.prognosis: With precursor replacement therapy many patients gain substantial and durable relief of orthostatic hypotension and can lead near-normal lives, which makes recognition important; untreated, disabling orthostatic symptoms persist, and perinatal presentations carry early morbidity.
pitfalls: Missing this treatable diagnosis in a young person with severe orthostatic hypotension
Not measuring plasma catecholamines to reveal the characteristic dopamine-to-noradrenaline profile
Confusing it with pure autonomic failure or multiple system atrophy
Overlooking supine hypertension that can arise during treatment
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
